claims.text: The onset and progression of phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles is governed by surface-diffusion-enabled selective dissolution of less-stable, non-noble elements.
Selective dissolution in bare FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles produces an early transient surface layer resembling a core-shell or passivating structure.
Formation of the transient surface layer accelerates progression to premelting and melting.
An externally applied robust passivation layer suppresses surface diffusion.
An externally applied robust passivation layer inhibits selective dissolution.
Passivation delays the phase transition and increases its onset-temperature threshold.
At elevated temperature, bare particles preferentially lose non-noble elements with lower reduction or dissolution potentials from their surfaces.
Preferential element loss rapidly modifies the surface atomic arrangement into a core-shell-type structure.
A noble or dissolution-resistant shell can passivate a nanoparticle and protect less-noble elements in its bulk from further dissolution.
The surface rearrangement caused by selective element loss locally lowers the effective melting point.
Local lowering of the effective melting point triggers the particle's phase transition.
Under identical heating conditions, bare nanoparticles will exhibit premelting or melting indicators at lower temperatures than passivated nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will retain their initial structure to higher temperatures than bare nanoparticles.
An inert atmosphere isolates the proposed transition mechanism from oxidation.
Nanoparticle size affects the transition because the surface-to-bulk atom ratio is important in the relevant size regime.
The magnitude and kinetics of the transition-temperature shift depend on nanoparticle size, composition, and passivation efficiency.
Identical transition onset, progression kinetics, surface-diffusion signals, and core-shell formation in bare and passivated particles would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial particles are described as disordered, but the prediction says passivated particles maintain their initial ordered structure.

A spontaneously formed passivating or core-shell surface layer is said to accelerate melting, whereas an applied passivation layer is said to inhibit the same surface processes and delay melting. The proposed distinction between these layers is not mechanistically resolved, and the cited evidence characterizes formed noble shells as stabilizing against dissolution.
